question: NPC: Writing a function the tests can see
intro: A woman in a chalk-dusted coat is drawing a box on the wall of the practice hall. “Good — a volunteer. Everything you have done so far was reading code. Now you write it, and the wall tells you whether it works.”

steps.say: Here is how these rounds go. I give you the first line of a function and say what it should answer. You write the inside. This one should add two numbers.

beats.say: Here is how these rounds go. I give you the first line of a function and say what it should answer.
You write the inside — only the inside. The def line is already on the wall above your box, and it does not change.

beats.code:
def add(a, b):
    # you write this part

steps.say: Now the part that catches everyone. The wall cannot see what your code prints. It can only see what your code returns.

beats.say: Now the part that catches everyone. The wall cannot read what your code prints on the floor. It can only catch what your code hands back.

check.prompt: So which line belongs in a function the tests will grade?
check.why: return hands the value back to whoever called the function. print only puts it on the screen, and a bare a + b works out the answer and then throws it away.

steps.say: When you are ready, press Run. The wall calls your function once for every example in the table and shows you what came back beside what it wanted.

beats.say: When you think it is right, press Run. The wall calls your function once for each example and shows what came back beside what it wanted.

beats.code:
add(1, 2)    wanted 3     you gave 3     ✔
add(5, 5)    wanted 10    you gave 10    ✔
add(-1, 1)   wanted 0     you gave -2    ✖

beats.say: That last row is a gift. It does not just say you are wrong — it says exactly which call goes wrong, so you know where to look.

check.prompt: Running the tests costs you nothing. How many times should you run before you submit?
check.why: Running is free and unlimited here. Only Submit puts you back in the fight, so try, read the failing row, fix, and try again until the table is all ticks.

steps.say: One last thing. Your code runs on a small Python that knows the first month of the language and says so plainly when something goes wrong. Read what it tells you — it names the line.

beats.say: One last thing. When something breaks, read the message. It names the line and says what happened in plain words.

beats.code:
line 2: You tried to add text and a number together.
        Use str(n) to make the number into text.

beats.say: A red table is not a verdict on you. It is the most patient tutor in the building, and it will sit there all evening. Off you go.

feedback: Write the body, return the answer, run as often as you like, and read the failing row before you change anything.

question: The party sleeps in when it is not a weekday, or when they are on holiday. Return True if they sleep in.
solution: return holiday or not weekday
feedback: Read the rule as one expression: not a weekday OR on holiday. Because the answer is already True or False, you can return the comparison itself — an if/else that returns True or False is doing the same work twice.

question: Return the sum of two numbers — except that if the two numbers are equal, return double their sum.
feedback: Handle the special case first and return from inside the if. Once a return runs, the rest of the function never does, so the ordinary case can simply sit underneath.

question: Return the absolute difference between n and 21 — except that if n is over 21, return double the absolute difference.
feedback: Under 21 the difference is 21 - n, which is already positive. Over 21 it is n - 21, doubled. Splitting on n > 21 means you never need abs() at all.

question: The parrot squawks in the early morning and the late evening. Return True if there is trouble: the parrot is talking, and the hour is before 7 or after 20.
solution: return talking and (hour < 7 or hour > 20)
feedback: The parentheses matter. `talking and hour < 7 or hour > 20` would be read as `(talking and hour < 7) or (hour > 20)`, which reports trouble at 11pm even when the parrot is silent, because and binds more tightly than or.

question: Return True if one of the two numbers is 10, or if their sum is 10.
solution: return a == 10 or b == 10 or a + b == 10
feedback: Three separate conditions joined by or. Note that a == 10 or b == 10 cannot be shortened to a or b == 10 — that would ask whether a is truthy, which is a different question.

question: Return True when n is within 10 of either 100 or 200. Within 10 means the distance is 10 or less.
solution: return abs(100 - n) <= 10 or abs(200 - n) <= 10
feedback: abs() turns a distance into a positive number, so one comparison covers both sides of each target. Without it you would need four comparisons.

question: Given a name, return a greeting of the form "Hello Bob!".
solution: return "Hello " + name + "!"
feedback: Text is joined with +, and the spaces have to be inside the quotes — "Hello" + name would run the words together. An f-string does the same job: f"Hello {name}!".

question: Given two strings a and b, return a string of the form a-b-b-a: the first, then the second twice, then the first again.
solution: return a + b + b + a
feedback: Nothing is repeated in the middle by accident: b + b really is the second string twice. b * 2 would do the same thing.

question: Return the first two characters of a string. If the string is shorter than two characters, return whatever is there.
solution: return s[:2]
feedback: A slice never complains about running off the end: "a"[:2] is just "a". That is why no if is needed here, while s[0] + s[1] would stop on a one-character string.

question: Return a string made of three copies of the last two characters of the given string. The string will be at least two characters long.
solution: return s[-2:] * 3
feedback: s[-2:] counts from the right-hand end, so it takes the last two characters whatever the length. Multiplying a string by 3 repeats it.

question: Given two strings, return the shorter one, then the longer one, then the shorter one again. The two strings are never the same length.
feedback: Only the order changes between the two cases, so decide which is shorter once and write the pattern twice rather than trying to work it out inside one expression.

question: Given a string, return a version without its first two characters, moved to the end. "Hello" becomes "lloHe". Strings of fewer than two characters come back unchanged.
feedback: Two slices that split at the same point: s[2:] is everything from position 2 onward, s[:2] is everything before it. Joined the other way round, they rotate the string.

question: Given a list of numbers, return True if 6 appears as either the first or the last number. The list will have at least one number in it.
solution: return nums[0] == 6 or nums[-1] == 6
feedback: nums[-1] is the last item, whatever the length — safer than nums[len(nums) - 1] and much shorter. A one-item list is both first and last at once, which is why [6] works.

question: Given two lists of numbers, return True if they have the same first number or the same last number. Both lists will have at least one number.
solution: return a[0] == b[0] or a[-1] == b[-1]
feedback: Compare ends to ends, not lists to lists: a == b would ask whether the whole lists match.

question: Given a list of exactly three numbers, return their sum.
solution: return nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[2]
feedback: Three known positions, so three lookups. Once the length can vary, a loop or sum(nums) does the same job without knowing how many there are.

question: Given a list of exactly three numbers, return a list of three copies of the larger of its first and last numbers.
solution:
biggest = max(nums[0], nums[-1])
return [biggest, biggest, biggest]
feedback: Work out the value once, put it in a variable, then build the list from it. Note the middle number is ignored entirely — only the two ends are compared.

question: Given two lists of exactly three numbers, return a new list of length two containing the middle number of each.
solution: return [a[1], b[1]]
feedback: Square brackets build a new list, and inside them a[1] and b[1] pick out position 1 — the middle of three, because counting starts at 0.

question: Given a list of numbers, return how many of them are even.
feedback: The accumulator pattern: start a counter at 0 before the loop, add to it inside, return it after. n % 2 == 0 is the test for even, and it works on negative numbers too.
starter:
count = 0
for n in nums:
    # decide whether to count n
return count

question: Return the sum of the numbers in a list, but ignore any number that is negative.
feedback: Same shape as counting, but the accumulator grows by n instead of by 1. An empty list returns 0, because the loop simply never runs.

question: Return the number of times the string "hi" appears anywhere in the given string.
feedback: Look at every two-character window in turn: s[i:i+2]. Stopping at len(s) - 1 keeps the last window from running off the end. (s.count("hi") does this in one step, once you know it exists.)

question: Return a string where every character of the given string appears twice: "The" becomes "TThhee".
solution:
out = ""
for ch in s:
    out += ch + ch
return out
feedback: An accumulator can build text as easily as it adds numbers: start with an empty string, add to it each time round, return it at the end.
starter:
out = ""
for ch in s:
    # add ch to out, twice
return out

question: Given a whole number that is zero or larger, return the sum of its digits. 512 gives 8.
solution:
total = 0
while n > 0:
    total += n % 10
    n = n // 10
return total
feedback: n % 10 peels off the last digit and n // 10 removes it, so the loop shortens the number each time round until nothing is left. Using / instead of // would give a decimal, and the loop would never reach 0.

question: Return the largest number in a list. The list will always have at least one number in it. Do not use max().
feedback: Start with the first number as the best guess, then replace it whenever something bigger turns up. Starting at 0 instead would give the wrong answer for a list of negatives.

question: Return True if the given string reads the same forwards and backwards, and False otherwise. The empty string reads the same either way.
solution: return s == s[::-1]
feedback: s[::-1] steps through the string backwards, giving a reversed copy. Comparing a string with its own reverse answers the question in one line.

question: Given a list of words, return a dictionary whose keys are the words and whose values are their lengths.
feedback: Start with an empty dictionary and add a key each time round the loop. sizes[word] = len(word) creates the key if it is new and overwrites it if it is not.
